title: What time is it? — and why "seven and a half" means 7:30
goal: Tell the time, name the days, and make appointments — and steer clear of the one-hour mix-up that catches Budi out.
bekal: tell any time of day accurately
name the days of the Iranian week, which starts on Saturday

dialogs.title: گفتگو — قرارِ فردا
dialogs.intro: Maryam calls Budi to set up a meeting at the language institute.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.id: Hi Budi. Do you have time tomorrow?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: سلام. بله، فردا آزادم. ساعتِ چند؟
lines.baca: salâm. bale, fardâ âzâdam. sâ'at-e chand?
lines.id: Hi. Yes, I'm free tomorrow. What time?
lines.literal: peace. yes, tomorrow free-I. hour-of how-many?

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: ساعتِ ده و نیمِ صبح خوب است؟
lines.baca: sâ'at-e dah o nim-e sobh khub ast?
lines.literal: hour-of ten and half-of morning good is?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.baca: bebakhshid, dah o nim ya'ni dah o si daghighe?
lines.literal: forgive, ten and half means ten and thirty minute?

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.baca: bale, dah o si. chetowr magar?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: در زبانِ ما "نیمِ ده" یعنی ۹:۳۰. همیشه اشتباه می‌کنم.

lines.baca: jâleb ast! pas dah o nim, na noh o nim.

lines.text: در کافهٔ مؤسسه. من معمولاً ساعتِ نه آنجا هستم.

notes: ⚠️⚠️ **This is the one-hour trap that catches Budi — and many Europeans.** Persian counts time **forward**: ده و نیم is literally "ten and a half" = **10:30**, just like English "half past ten" (or British "half ten"). Indonesian, German, and Dutch count **backward**: "half ten" there means 9:30, halfway *toward* ten. Same words, two times a full hour apart.

⚠️ **The Iranian week starts on Saturday.** Saturday (شنبه) is the first working day, and the weekly day off is **Friday (جمعه)** — with Thursday (پنج‌شنبه) often a half day or a day off too. Sunday (یکشنبه) is an ordinary working day. Book something for "the weekend" without naming the day, and you and the other person are talking about two different things.

**The word یعنی = "it means, that is".** You'll use it dozens of times a day while learning: این یعنی چه؟ ("what does this mean?"), and on its own یعنی چه؟ ("what do you mean?"). It's an Arabic loan, and Persian speakers drop it into sentences the way English speakers say "I mean…".
**The phrase چطور مگر؟ = "why do you ask?"** A casual way to ask the reason behind someone's question. Polite, light, and very common.

***Rowshan shod*** **(روشن شد) = "got it"**, literally "it became bright". You met روشن in unit 5 as "bright"; here it is used for understanding — just as English says "it's clear now" or "that sheds light on it".
**Spoken forms:** ساعت چنده؟ (*sâ'at chande?*), ده و نیمِ صبح خوبه؟ (*dah o nim-e sobh khube?*), فردا چه روزیه؟ (*fardâ che ruziye?*), تعطیلیم (*ta'tilim* — unchanged).

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Every time expression starts with ساعت ("hour"), then the number, then any minutes. To ask the time: **ساعت چند است؟**
after: **Up to half past, use و ("and"); after that, use به or کم.** The line falls at about the 30-minute mark: past it, Iranians prefer to count down to the next hour — just like English "past" and "to".

⚠️ Once more, because this one is costly: **هفت و نیم = 7:30, not 6:30.** If you have learned German or Dutch "half seven" (= 6:30), switch it off here, or you will turn up an hour early — or an hour late, depending on who got it wrong.

The part of the day is attached with ezafe: هفتِ صبح ("seven in the morning"), سهِ بعدازظهر ("three in the afternoon"), نهِ شب ("nine at night"). Iran uses the 24-hour clock in official timetables, but everyday speech uses the 12-hour clock plus the part of the day.

grammars.title: The days, and a week that starts on Saturday
after: ⚠️ **Friday (جمعه) is Iran's day off, not Sunday.** Offices, schools, and most shops are closed, while museums and sights are packed. If you have official business, don't schedule it for a Friday.
In Iran, **آخرِ هفته** ("the weekend") means Thursday and Friday, and **اولِ هفته** ("the start of the week") means Saturday.
To say "on Fridays", make it plural: جمعه‌ها (*jom'e-hâ*). You saw this in unit 5.

grammars.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow
after: Notice the prefix **ام** ("this") in امروز ("today"), امشب ("tonight") and امسال ("this year") — all meaning "the current one". And the prefix **دی** in دیروز and دیشب means "the one just past".

blocks.text: The word **قرار** (*gharâr*) means "appointment". قرار داشتن = "to have an appointment", قرار گذاشتن = "to make an appointment", and قرارمان ساعتِ ده = "our appointment is at ten".

blocks.title: Time in Iran: what really happens
items: ⚠️ **Social times in Iran are loose; official ones are not.** Arriving at a dinner invitation at exactly eight is actually too early — your hosts may not be ready. But appointments with an office, a doctor, or a bank mean exactly what they say.

A word you will hear at the end of every plan: **ایشالله** (*ishâllâ*, from ان‌شاءالله), "God willing". It carries the same layers it has across the Muslim world: sincere, but not fully binding — a bit like "hopefully" in English.

blocks.title: Three dates that bring all of Iran to a halt
items: **1 Farvardin (۱ فروردین) — Nowruz (نوروز)**, the Persian New Year and the biggest holiday. The whole country stops for about two weeks, offices close, and everyone travels. Don't plan any business for the first two weeks of Farvardin.
**13 Farvardin (۱۳ فروردین) — Sizdah Bedar (سیزده‌بدر)**, the thirteenth day of the new year: everyone must leave the house and have a picnic. The cities empty, the parks fill up.

**Tasua and Ashura (تاسوعا و عاشورا)** in the month of Muharram (محرم; on the Islamic lunar calendar, so the dates shift every year) — two days of mourning for Imam Hossein. Many shops and restaurants close, and the streets fill with processions.

ساعت چند است؟ — فردا وقت دارید؟ — قرارمان ساعتِ ده و نیم است. — جمعه تعطیل است. — فردا چهارشنبه است.
